sections.report:
**Walk (working notes).** The image is about one screen (about 1280×800), so I worked from the whole image. Bash is denied, so I couldn't run the crop script or the entries script, and I judged from the image and checklist wording alone.

First read: the eye goes to the large blue headline, then the "Create your link" button, then along the four blue-outlined cards. It's a SaaS landing page for a booking-link tool, aimed at small service businesses. It feels clean and safe, but everything is the same blue, so after the headline nothing pulls ahead.

1. One-sentence purpose: yes.
2. Image and headline make one idea: yes, because there is no main image. The empty right half of the hero is noted under "Couldn't judge."
3. Every element does a job: no. The four heavy blue card outlines, the "Auto" and "Email" badges, and four identical "Learn more" links.
4. One mood and era: yes.
5. Copy finished: yes.
6. Repeated elements look the same: no. Card 1's title wraps and its badge sits right-aligned, so its "Learn more" drops to y≈672 while the others sit at y≈642.
7. Colours and shapes carry the mood: yes.
8. Headings name their section: no. The name strip at y≈770 has no heading.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something?**
   - **Where:** the four cards at y≈430–710 each have a 2 px saturated-blue outline, the same blue as the headline, buttons, links, titles, icons and badges. The badges "Auto" (x≈507–553) and "Email" (x≈793–843) just restate the card title ("Time zones" are automatic, "Reminders" are email). Each card ends in an identical "Learn more" link.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** the outlines draw a heavy border around every feature, so the feature row has as much visual weight as the hero. The eye gets pulled down from "Create your link" into four equal boxes. "New" and "Beta" tell the viewer something; "Auto" and "Email" look like status flags but carry no status, so they're noise. The four "Learn more" links give the viewer four identical targets with no sense of where each one goes.
   - **Why:** this is the reduction principle: a box or rule where space would do adds weight without meaning (Refactoring UI; Nielsen heuristic 8, aesthetic and minimalist design). Unverified: I couldn't open the catalog entries.
   - **Fix:** drop the outlines or make them a pale neutral, so the cards group by spacing and the primary button stays the strongest blue below the headline. Keep badges only where they mark a real state (New, Beta). Make the links specific, or make the whole card the link.
   - Defect (the cards compete with the primary call to action). **Weight: major.**
2. **Within one screen or image, does each kind of element (primary buttons, links, cards, section headings, error states) look the same everywhere it appears?**
   - **Where:** card 1, "Shared calendars" (x≈90–250, y≈515–570). The title wraps onto two lines and the "New" badge is pushed to the right edge (x≈264–308), while the other three cards put the badge right after a one-line title. As a result, card 1's body text starts about 30 px lower, and its "Learn more" sits at y≈672 against y≈642 in cards 2–4.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** the row's baselines are broken at the first card, the one read first. It looks like a bug rather than a design choice.
   - **Why:** repeated elements should follow one program (Nielsen heuristic 4, consistency and standards).
   - **Fix:** make all four titles fit on one line, either with a shorter title (e.g. "Team calendars") or by letting the badge wrap under the title. Then pin the links to a shared baseline.
   - Defect. **Weight: minor.**
3. **Does each heading name what its section holds?**
   - **Where:** the strip below the rule at y≈740–780 ("Harbor Dental, Northfield Tutoring, Kestrel Physio, Lumen Coaching, Orchard Vets").
   - **What the viewer experiences:** five business names in small grey text with no heading or logos. A stranger has to guess that these are customers. As plain text, they don't work as social proof: the viewer can't tell whether these are customers, partners or sample data.
   - **Fix:** add a short heading such as "Used by clinics, tutors and coaches", or show the real logos, so the strip reads as proof.
   - This is common sense; no catalog entry was opened. Defect. **Weight: minor.**

**Copy notes (no checklist line).**
- "Booking links that fill your calendar" could sit on any scheduling product's page. It's a category claim with nothing that sets this product apart, so the viewer can't tell why to pick it over the tool they already use.
- The subhead is clear, and "Create your link" is a good, exact ask.
- Neither line compares the product with what the viewer does today (the back-and-forth email thread), which would let them judge the value for themselves.
- Taste. Weight: major for a landing page whose job is to win a switch.

**What's working.**
- The purpose reads in one glance. The headline, subhead and "Create your link" together say what this is and what to do next, in plain words.
- One sans family, one blue and one rounded-corner shape language give the page a single coherent mood with no collage effect.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- The right half of the hero (about x 660–1216, y 100–380) is empty. On a page like this, that space usually holds a product picture. If one should be there and didn't load in the capture, check a live browser. If it's meant to be empty, the arrangement critic should weigh it.
- Where the four "Learn more" links go, and whether the cards are clickable as a whole.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 5 yes, 3 no (every element does a job; repeated elements look the same; headings name their section), 0 unsure. The step 1 crop script and the step 5 entries script couldn't be run because Bash was denied, so these answers come from the image and the checklist wording alone, not the catalog entries.

After the deep read, every line in this section comes out yes. Here is the report.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

The only line I had to check closely was the second one. The lead paragraph (y≈245–295, looks about 19 px, regular, dark grey) and the card titles (y≈515–570, look about 20 px, bold, blue) are close in size. They still read as different levels at a glance because they also differ in weight and colour, and they sit in separate zones of the page. That is the obvious contrast Dair asks for, not the one-step difference he warns against. The card body (about 15 px) and the customer-name strip at y≈770 (about 14 px, grey) are also close in size, but they are different kinds of text in separate places, not two paragraph blocks that clash. If the designer tightens the type scale, the 19/20 and 14/15 pairs are the ones to merge. The measurements to take are the font sizes of the lead paragraph, a card title, the card body and the customer names.

**What's working.**
- The headline "Booking links that fill your calendar" (x≈64–645, y≈120–225, looks about 48 px bold) is more than twice the size of anything else on the page. The eye has one place to start and doesn't have to search.
- The order runs cleanly: headline, then lead line, then the solid "Create your link" button paired with a lighter text link, then the cards. The card headings differ from their body in weight and colour as well as size, so each card is easy to skim.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

I reviewed the Arrangement and space section. Bash was denied, so I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts. I judged from the whole image (about one screen, 1280×800) and opened `references/layout.md` directly. I didn't open the entries in typography.md, basics.md or art-direction.md. Pixel positions are estimated from the image, not measured.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** Also **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas?** These are one problem.
   - **Where:** All the weight in the hero sits in the left half: the headline, the subhead and the button, roughly x 64–645, y 120–380. The right half, roughly x 660–1216, y 90–400, is empty white.
   - **What the viewer sees:** The empty half is the biggest open area on the page but does no work. Nothing balances the heavy blue headline, so the page leans left. On a landing page for a booking product, a blank area that size reads as a product picture that failed to load, not as chosen space. The viewer never sees a booking page, which is the thing being sold.
   - **Why:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance": a heavy side needs a counterweight. Ruder, *Typography: A Manual of Design*, "Contrasts": empty space should be shaped against dense areas, not left over.
   - **Fix:** Put a counterweight on the right, most usefully a picture of the booking page a guest would see. Or, if the space is meant to stay empty, give it a shape, for example a centred hero or a wider hero text column.
   - **What would make this fine:** if a hero image exists and didn't load in the capture, this isn't a finding. Check it in a live browser.
   - **Rating:** Defect. Major.
2. **Do lines of text in neighboring columns sit on the same baselines?**
   - **Where:** In the first card (x 64–333), "Shared calendars" wraps to two lines. That pushes its body text down to about y 590 and "Learn more" to about y 672. In the other three cards they sit at about y 560 and y 642.
   - **What the viewer sees:** The row of four cards breaks in its first column. The eye reads the first card as a different design, and the line of "Learn more" links staggers.
   - **Why:** Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*: lines of text align across columns. Gerstner, *Designing Programmes*: matching elements follow one program.
   - **Fix:** Keep every card title to one line, for example a shorter title or the badge on its own line in every card. Or pin the title, body and link rows to the same heights in all four cards.
   - **Rating:** Defect. Minor.
3. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?**
   - **Badge:** In card 1 the "New" badge is pushed to the card's right edge (about x 264–308) and centred between two title lines. In cards 2–4 the badge follows the title on its baseline. The same element has two placements that differ only slightly.
   - **Nav:** The link group (Product to Docs, about x 474–781) looks centred in the space between the logo and the button, with its midpoint near x 627. The page's axis is x 640, and the gutter between cards 2 and 3 is centred there. So the nav looks about 12 px off the page's centre line. It's close enough to look meant to line up, and off enough to look like a miss. This is by eye; measure it.
   - **Why:** Arnheim, ch. I "Balance": a placement that is almost aligned makes the eye waver.
   - **Fix:** Put the badge in the same place in every card. Centre the nav on the page axis, or move it clearly away from centre, for example next to the logo.
   - **Rating:** Taste. Minor.
4. **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over in scattered small gaps?** This is the smaller second half of finding 1.
   - **Where:** Cards 2–4 have about 55 px of empty space below "Learn more" (y 655–708). Card 1 has about 25 px.
   - **What the viewer sees:** The equal-height cards hold uneven leftover space, which makes the row look slightly unfinished.
   - **Fix:** This goes away when finding 2 is fixed.
   - **Rating:** Taste. Minor.

**What's working.**
- The content sits on one clear four-column grid. The card edges at about 64/333, 358/627, 652/921 and 946/1215 have equal gutters of about 25 px. The logo, the headline, the first card, the rule and the first customer name all share the left edge at x 64, and the "Start free" button ends near x 1216, where the cards end. The page reads as built, not placed by eye.
- Inside each card, the spacing groups the content well. The icon, the title, the body and the link step down with gaps tighter than the card's own padding, so each card reads as one unit.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the empty right half of the hero is meant to hold an image that didn't load.
- How the four cards reflow at narrower widths, where the title wrap in finding 2 will likely spread to other cards.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 9 yes, 4 no (visual weight balances; empty space gathered; baselines align across columns; no near-miss alignment).

sections.report:
**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name? No.** There are two cases.
   - **The hero headline (x 64–645, y 120–225).** It breaks "Booking links that fill your / calendar", so "calendar" sits alone on line 2 and the break splits "your calendar". The headline reads as a long line with one word left over, not two balanced lines. Its biggest blue mass is the top line, and "calendar", the word that says where the bookings go, gets the least weight.
   - **The first card title (x 90–187, y 515–568).** It splits the feature name "Shared / calendars". This is the only card title on two lines, because the "New" badge (x 264–308) takes the width the title needs. The badge then sits centred on both lines, away from the title. The title's wrap pushes that card's body text and "Learn more" (y≈672) about 30 px below the other three cards' (y≈642), so the row's text baselines don't line up.

   The approved sources don't cover breaks in headings (the entry marks that part unconfirmed), so this is a judgment call, not a rule.

   Direction of the fix:
   - Headline: break it at the phrase, for example "Booking links that / fill your calendar". Or widen the box so it sits on one line, or set the break by hand.
   - Card: keep "Shared calendars" on one line. Move the badge below or above the title, shorten the name, or let the title use the badge's width.

   Classification: taste. Weight: minor. The page still reads, but the uneven card row is the one visible flaw on an otherwise tidy hero.

**What's working.**
- **One sans family, set mainly through weight and colour.** The blue bold headline, grey regular subhead, blue bold card titles and grey regular card text use a few sizes with clear jobs. Nothing reads as a near-miss size or a second face.
- **Short, legible text blocks.** The subhead runs ~65 characters a line, well inside the 45–75 range Bringhurst gives. Each card blurb is three short lines with comfortable line spacing, so the page scans quickly.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Bash was refused, so I couldn't zoom. I read the badge text ("New", "Auto", "Email", "Beta", ~12 px white on blue) and the grey customer names (y≈770) from the full 1280×800 image. Both look readable, but contrast should be measured in a browser.
- The headline and card-title breaks depend on viewport width. Check them at the real breakpoints, because they may land differently.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (headings break at phrase boundaries).

sections.report:
**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is strong, saturated color kept to a small share of the area, with most of the area neutral or muted?** No. By area the page is mostly white, but the same saturated blue sits on almost every element: the logo-row nav links (474–781, 30), the "Start free" button (1107–1216, 10–52), the two-line headline (64–645, 120–220), the "Create your link" button (64–247, 325–378), the "See a live example" link, the 2px outlines of all four cards (64–1216, 430–710), the four icons, the four card titles, the four pill badges ("New", "Auto", "Email", "Beta"), the four "Learn more" links, and the full-width rule at y≈740. The viewer gets no signal from the color. The headline, the card titles and the card borders are all the same blue as the primary CTA, so "Create your link" is one blue thing among about 25 and doesn't stand out as the action. Blue also stops meaning "clickable": the card titles and headline look like links next to the "Learn more" links. The four outlined cards add up to a heavy blue band in the lower half that pulls the eye away from the hero CTA. This breaks accent color restraint: one accent kept for the main action and interactive state, not used to decorate content that isn't interactive (Apple HIG, Color; Material Design 3, Color roles). This page is the entry's "how bad it gets" case: accent on headings, icons, borders, tags and links as well as on the main action. Fix: keep the blue for the buttons, the links and at most one highlight. Set the headline and card titles in the dark neutral of the body text, make the card outlines a light gray hairline or drop them, turn the icons gray, and make the badges a light blue tint or gray chip. Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- The palette is tight: one blue, a dark gray for text, a mid gray for the customer names, and white. There are no stray one-off hues, so the page reads as one system and the blue is plainly the brand color.
- Value carries the structure. Dark text and saturated blue on white keep the hierarchy readable in grayscale, and none of the colors touch each other at similar lightness, so no edge vibrates.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 8 yes, 1 no (strong color kept to a small share: the accent blue is on almost every element)

sections.report:
**Section.** Pictures: applies. The pictures are the four feature icons (y ≈ 458–490) and the "Slotwise" wordmark. There are no photos or illustrations. I couldn't run the crop script (Bash was denied), so I judged everything from the whole 1280×800 image.

**Findings**
1. **Do the pictures share one rendering style and one level of detail? / Do the icons and line drawings share one stroke weight, cap style, and corner radius?** The four card icons don't match. Shared calendars (x ≈ 94–122) is a thin outline with an open, hollow face. Time zones (x ≈ 386–418) is a solid filled disc. Reminders (x ≈ 680–712) is a solid envelope. Intake forms (x ≈ 976–1002) is three solid square-cornered blocks. The row is meant to be one matched set, so the calendar looks lighter and older than the other three, and the set looks pieced together from different icon packs rather than designed together. That small seam weakens the polish of the page's main feature area. The approved fix (Apple Human Interface Guidelines, "Icons") is to redraw or replace the odd icons so the whole set shares one level of detail and one stroke weight. Here that means all outline or all filled, from one family, with one corner radius. Convention. Weight: minor.
2. **Extra finding, not on the checklist: the Intake forms icon doesn't show a form.** At x ≈ 976–1002, y ≈ 462–486, the glyph is a header bar over two blocks, which reads as a page layout or dashboard. Nothing in it suggests questions or fields. The other three icons show their feature in a literal way (calendar, clock, envelope), so this one makes the viewer stop and decode it. Swap it for a clipboard or a form with fields and a checkbox. Taste (common sense). Weight: minor.

**What's working.** The icons all use one brand blue at one size and sit in the same spot in every card, top left above the title. Because of that, the mismatch in style is the only thing breaking the set, and it's a cheap fix. The "Slotwise" wordmark has plenty of clear space in the header and is a plain dark wordmark that will still read small and in one colour.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The right half of the hero (about x 680–1216, y 100–400) is empty. It may be deliberate white space, or it may be a hero image or product screenshot that hadn't loaded when the screenshot was taken. Check in a live browser. If an image should be there, this is a missing-picture defect, not a layout choice. Also, the customer strip at y ≈ 770 is plain-text names, not logos. If logos are supposed to show there, check that they load.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 10 yes, 2 no (one rendering style and level of detail; one stroke weight, cap style and corner radius), 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has a nav bar, two filled buttons, a text link, four "Learn more" links and four bordered feature cards.

**Findings**
1. **Does every control look like what it does, buttons pressable, fields typeable, and links marked by more than color?** One saturated blue is used for the H1 (64–645, 120–225), the four card titles, the 2 px card borders, the four pill badges ("New", "Auto", "Email", "Beta" at about y 515–540), the nav links, the text links and both buttons. Because everything is blue, the colour stops telling the viewer what can be clicked. The filled badges look like small buttons. A blue title inside a blue-bordered box reads as one big clickable card, but the only real target is the underlined "Learn more" at the bottom. People will click the title or the badge and nothing will happen, or they won't know where to click (Norman, *The Design of Everyday Things*: affordances and signifiers, where things that can't be used shouldn't look usable). Fix: keep the strong blue for things you can act on. Set the H1 and card titles in the dark text colour. Give the cards a neutral grey border, or make the whole card one link. Make the badges look like status labels: a tint or outline, smaller, not a solid fill. Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Do the navigation and components follow the conventions users know from the platform and similar products?** The header (0–63) has the logo, Product / Pricing / Customers / Docs and "Start free", but no "Log in" or "Sign in". On a SaaS marketing page, returning users expect sign-in at the top right next to the main button. Here a returning user is left hunting, or clicks "Start free" and ends up in a sign-up flow (Nielsen, heuristic 4, Consistency and standards). Fix: add a quiet "Log in" text link just left of "Start free". Convention. Weight: minor for the page's main job of winning new users, but annoying for every existing customer.
3. **Do the grouping, names, and navigation show how the product's parts relate?** The four badges look identical but mean different kinds of things. "New" and "Beta" describe how far along a feature is. "Auto" and "Email" describe how a feature works. The reader can't learn what a badge means, and "Beta" loses its warning value when it looks the same as "Email" (Norman, *The Design of Everyday Things*: conceptual model). Fix: use badges only for status (New, Beta). Move "automatic" and "by email" into the card descriptions. Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- There is a clear pair of actions in the hero. "Create your link" (64–247, 325–378) is a filled button and "See a live example" is an underlined text link beside it. The main and second actions differ in weight, and both labels say exactly what happens next. Keep that pairing.
- The text links are underlined, so they don't depend on colour alone. Each "Learn more" sits at the foot of its own card, which makes its purpose clear from context (WCAG 2.4.4).

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus indicators on the nav links, buttons and "Learn more" links. With this much blue on the page, a blue focus ring may not stand out. Tab through the page live to check.
- Hover states on the cards. If the whole card highlights on hover but only "Learn more" is a link, finding 1 gets worse.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 28 yes, 3 no (controls look like what they do; platform and product conventions; grouping and names show how parts relate), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not covered)
